claim: Cylicin-1 is specifically expressed in testis tissues according to the Expression Atlas database.
source: According to the Expression Atlas database, cylicin-1 was specifically expressed in testis tissues, and restricted to early and late spermatid subpopulations (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to the Expression Atlas database and is illustrated in figures.

claim: Cylicin-1 is restricted to early and late spermatid subpopulations within the testis.
source: According to the Expression Atlas database, cylicin-1 was specifically expressed in testis tissues, and restricted to early and late spermatid subpopulations (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by database information and figure references showing expression patterns.

claim: Cylicin-1 was initially expressed at the subacrosomal layer (SAL) in round and elongating spermatids.
source: Using our homemade rabbit anti-CYLC1 antibody (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), we showed that cylicin-1 was initially expressed at the subacrosomal layer (SAL) in round and elongating spermatids and then translocated to the postacrosomal region (PAR) in sperm (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data using an anti-CYLC1 antibody.

claim: Cylicin-1 translocates from the subacrosomal layer to the postacrosomal region (PAR) in sperm.
source: Using our homemade rabbit anti-CYLC1 antibody (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), we showed that cylicin-1 was initially expressed at the subacrosomal layer (SAL) in round and elongating spermatids and then translocated to the postacrosomal region (PAR) in sperm (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing dynamic localization during spermiogenesis.

claim: The dynamic expression pattern of cylicin-1 is similar to that of CAPZA3, calicin, and ACTRT1, all showing SAL-to-PAR translocation during spermiogenesis.
source: The dynamic expression pattern of cylicin-1 is quite similar to that of CAPZA3 (von Bülow et al., 1997), calicin (Zhang et al., 2022a), and ACTRT1 (Zhang et al., 2022b), all showing SAL-to-PAR translocation during spermiogenesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with published data on other proteins.

claim: Cylc1-KO mice were generated by deleting a 3651-bp region containing exons 3 and 4 of the Cylc1 gene using CRISPR/Cas9 technology.
source: The Cylc1 gene has only one transcript and a 3651-bp region containing exons 3 and 4 was selected as the knockout region (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the knockout strategy and confirmed by sequencing data.

claim: Western blotting analysis confirmed the absence of cylicin-1 protein in the testis of Cylc1-KO mice.
source: Western blotting analysis with anti-cylicin-1 antibody confirmed absence of the cylicin-1 in the testis protein lysates of Cylc1-KO mice (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data showing no protein expression in knockout mice.

claim: Cylc1-KO male mice suffered from severe male subfertility.
source: Although Cylc1-KO male mice were able to mate normally with females, they suffered from severe male subfertility.
evidence: The claim is supported by fertility testing data showing reduced pregnancy rates and offspring numbers.

claim: Both the pregnancy rates of mating females and pups born from Cylc1-KO males were significantly reduced compared with those from WT males.
source: Both the pregnancy rates of mating females and pups that were born from Cylc1-KO males were significantly reduced compared with those from WT males (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative fertility testing data.

claim: The testis size and weight were similar between Cylc1-KO mice and their littermate WT mice.
source: The testis size and weight were similar between Cylc1-KO mice and their littermate WT mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological measurements and statistical analysis.

claim: Histological examination of Cylc1-KO testis and cauda epididymis revealed generally normal spermatogenesis and sperm production.
source: Histological examination of Cylc1-KO testis and cauda epididymis revealed generally normal spermatogenesis and sperm production (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological analysis using H&E staining.

claim: Both the sperm count and the total motility were similar between Cylc1-KO mice and WT mice.
source: Both the sperm count and the total motility were similar between Cylc1-KO mice and WT mice (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative sperm analysis using CASA.

claim: Cylc1-KO mice produced sperm with abnormal head morphologies, exhibiting varying degrees of 'fan-shaped' heads.
source: The sperm of WT mice showed a typical 'hook-shaped' appearance with a streamlined dorsal part (Figure 1F), whereas the Cylc1-KO mice produced sperm with abnormal head morphologies, exhibiting varying degrees of 'fan-shaped' heads (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by Papanicolaou staining and microscopy analysis.

claim: Sperm with mild and severe 'fan-shaped' heads accounted for approximately 60% and 40% of the total sperm in Cylc1-KO mice, respectively.
source: Sperm with mild and severe 'fan-shaped' heads accounted for approximately 60% and 40% of the total sperm in Cylc1-KO mice, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative morphological analysis of sperm.

claim: Spermatids of Cylc1-KO mice exhibited varying degrees of acrosome detachment from the nuclear envelope.
source: In spermatids of WT mice, the developing acrosome was tightly bound to the NE of the sperm nucleus. Spermatids of Cylc1-KO mice, by contrast, exhibited varying degrees of acrosome detachment from the NE (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by PNA-FITC staining and fluorescence microscopy.

claim: The ratio of acrosome detachment in spermatids of Cylc1-KO mice was significantly higher than that in WT mice.
source: Statistical analysis indicated that the ratio of acrosome detachment in spermatids of Cylc1-KO mice was significantly higher than that in WT mice (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative statistical analysis of microscopy data.

claim: Spermatids of Cylc1-KO mice showed a disturbance of the PT-SAL distribution, and sometimes it broke away from the nuclear envelope.
source: Compared with WT mice, spermatids of Cylc1-KO mice showed a disturbance of the PT-SAL distribution, and sometimes it broke away from the NE (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by F-actin fluorescence probe staining.

claim: The percentage of spermatids with abnormal PT-SAL structure in Cylc1-KO mice was significantly greater than that in WT mice.
source: The percentage of spermatids with abnormal PT-SAL structure in Cylc1-KO mice was also significantly greater than that in WT mice (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of fluorescence microscopy data.

claim: The number of sperm with detached acrosomes was significantly higher in Cylc1-KO mice than in WT mice as revealed by TEM.
source: The number of sperm with detached acrosomes was significantly higher in Cylc1-KO mice than in WT mice (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative TEM analysis.

claim: TEM analysis revealed an enlarged space area between the IAM and the NE in spermatids of Cylc1-KO mice.
source: TEM analysis clearly revealed an enlarged space area between the IAM and the NE in spermatids of Cylc1-KO mice (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM imaging of testis tissues.

claim: The average PT-SAL thickness was significantly larger in the spermatids of Cylc1-KO mice than in WT mice.
source: The average PT-SAL thickness (space between the IAM and the NE) was significantly larger in the spermatids of Cylc1-KO mice than those of in WT mice (Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements from TEM images.

claim: The manchette was generally normal in the spermatids of Cylc1-KO mice.
source: Moreover, the manchette was generally normal in the spermatids of Cylc1-KO mice, as revealed by tubulin fluorescence probe staining and TEM analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by tubulin staining and TEM analysis.

claim: There was no difference in the ratio of spontaneous acrosome reaction in sperm between WT mice and Cylc1-KO mice.
source: There was no difference in the ratio of spontaneous AR in sperm between WT mice and Cylc1-KO mice; however, the calcium ionophore A23187-induced AR rate in sperm was significantly lower in Cylc1-KO mice than in WT mice (Figure 2I).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative acrosome reaction assays.

claim: The calcium ionophore A23187-induced acrosome reaction rate in sperm was significantly lower in Cylc1-KO mice than in WT mice.
source: There was no difference in the ratio of spontaneous AR in sperm between WT mice and Cylc1-KO mice; however, the calcium ionophore A23187-induced AR rate in sperm was significantly lower in Cylc1-KO mice than in WT mice (Figure 2I).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative acrosome reaction assays using A23187.

claim: The percentage of two-cell embryos using sperm of Cylc1-KO mice was significantly decreased compared with that of WT mice in IVF experiments.
source: The percentage of two-cell embryos using sperm of Cylc1-KO mice was significantly decreased compared with that of WT mice (Figure 2J).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro fertilization assay data.

claim: Cylicin-1 interacts with itself as demonstrated by coimmunoprecipitation in HEK293T cells.
source: First, we found that FLAG-tagged CYLC1 could be coimmunoprecipitated with Myc-tagged CYLC1 in HEK293T cells, demonstrating that cylicin-1 interacts with itself (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-IP experiments in cell culture.

claim: Cylicin-1 interacts with ACTRT1, ACTRT2, ACTL7A, CAPZA3, and CCIN as revealed by coimmunoprecipitation assays in HEK293T cells.
source: The interactions between Myc-tagged CYLC1 and several other FLAG-tagged PT proteins, such as ACTRT1, ACTRT2, ACTL7A, CAPZA3, and CCIN, were further revealed by coimmunoprecipitation (co-IP) assays in HEK293T cells (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-IP experiments in cell culture.

claim: The ACTL7A–CYLC1 interaction was confirmed by endogenous co-IP assay using mouse testis extracts.
source: The ACTL7A–CYLC1 interaction was further confirmed by endogenous co-IP assay using mouse testis extracts (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by endogenous co-IP experiments using tissue lysates.

claim: MST analysis indicated a binding affinity between GFP-labelled CYLC1 and purified ACTL7A in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Moreover, microscale thermophoresis (MST) analysis indicated a binding affinity between GFP-labelled CYLC1 and purified ACTL7A in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by MST binding assay data.

claim: The protein levels of PT proteins (ACTRT1, ACTRT2, ACTL7A, CCIN, CAPZA3, CAPZB, CYLC2, and PLCζ) were similar in the sperm sample between WT mice and Cylc1-KO mice.
source: The protein levels of PT proteins, such as ACTRT1, ACTRT2, ACTL7A, CCIN, CAPZA3, CAPZB, CYLC2, and PLCζ, were similar in the sperm sample between WT mice and Cylc1-KO mice, indicating that the sperm acrosome detachment in Cylc1-KO mice may not be due to altered PT protein contents (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot analysis of sperm protein lysates.

claim: The endogenous interaction between ACTRT1 and ACTL7A was partially disrupted by the loss of cylicin-1.
source: We found that the endogenous interaction between ACTRT1 and ACTL7A was partially disrupted by the loss of cylicin-1 (Figure 3D), highlighting the assistant role of cylicin-1 on the ACTRT1–ACTL7A connection.
evidence: The claim is supported by endogenous co-IP experiments comparing WT and Cylc1-KO mice.

claim: Myc-tagged CYLC1 was immunoprecipitated with the FLAG-tagged NE protein FAM209 in HEK293T cells.
source: We showed that Myc-tagged CYLC1 was immunoprecipitated with the FLAG-tagged NE protein FAM209 in HEK293T cells (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-IP experiments in cell culture.

claim: The interaction between CYLC1 and FAM209 was confirmed by endogenous co-IP using mouse testis extracts.
source: The interaction between CYLC1 and FAM209 was further confirmed by endogenous co-IP using mouse testis extracts (Figure 3F) and MST analysis using GFP-FAM209 cell lysates and purified CYLC1 (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by endogenous co-IP experiments using tissue lysates.

claim: MST analysis confirmed the interaction between CYLC1 and FAM209 using GFP-FAM209 cell lysates and purified CYLC1.
source: The interaction between CYLC1 and FAM209 was further confirmed by endogenous co-IP using mouse testis extracts (Figure 3F) and MST analysis using GFP-FAM209 cell lysates and purified CYLC1 (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by MST binding assay data.

claim: FLAG-tagged CYLC1 was immunoprecipitated with the Myc-tagged IAM protein SPACA1 in HEK293T cells.
source: We further found that FLAG-tagged CYLC1 was immunoprecipitated with the Myc-tagged IAM protein SPACA1 in HEK293T cells (Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-IP experiments in cell culture.

claim: The interaction between CYLC1 and SPACA1 was confirmed by endogenous co-IP using mouse testis extracts.
source: The interaction between CYLC1 and SPACA1 was further confirmed by endogenous co-IP using mouse testis extracts (Figure 3I) and a dose-dependent binding affinity between GFP-SPACA1 from cell lysates and recombinant CYLC1 by MST (Figure 3J).
evidence: The claim is supported by endogenous co-IP experiments using tissue lysates.

claim: MST analysis showed a dose-dependent binding affinity between GFP-SPACA1 from cell lysates and recombinant CYLC1.
source: The interaction between CYLC1 and SPACA1 was further confirmed by endogenous co-IP using mouse testis extracts (Figure 3I) and a dose-dependent binding affinity between GFP-SPACA1 from cell lysates and recombinant CYLC1 by MST (Figure 3J).
evidence: The claim is supported by MST binding assay data.

claim: Loss of cylicin-1 partially disrupted the IAM and PT-SAL connections because the interaction between SPACA1 and ACTL7A was weakened in Cylc1-KO mice.
source: Loss of cylicin-1 partially disrupted the IAM and PT-SAL connections because the interaction between SPACA1 and ACTL7A was weakened in Cylc1-KO mice, as revealed by an endogenous co-IP assay using mouse testis extracts (Figure 3K).
evidence: The claim is supported by endogenous co-IP experiments comparing WT and Cylc1-KO mice.

claim: WES analysis was performed in a large cohort of more than 500 infertile patients with sperm head deformities.
source: To explore the clinical relevance of cylicin-1 deficiency to human male infertility, we performed WES analysis in a large cohort of more than 500 infertile patients with sperm head deformities (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the WES study design.

claim: Nineteen individuals were identified to harbor a variant of CYLC1 (c.1377G>T/p.K459N).
source: Intriguingly, 19 individuals were identified to harbor a variant of CYLC1 (GenBank: NM_021118.3): c.1377G>T/p.K459N (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by WES data and Sanger sequencing confirmation.

claim: The CYLC1 variant (c.1377G>T/p.K459N) was predicted to be deleterious through utilization of SIFT, PolyPhen-2, and CADD.
source: The variant was predicted to be deleterious through utilization of SIFT (Ng and Henikoff, 2003), PolyPhen-2 (Adzhubei et al., 2013), and CADD (Rentzsch et al., 2019; Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational prediction tools and cited references.

claim: The amino acid residue of the CYLC1 variant was conserved between humans and mice.
source: Moreover, the amino acid residue of this variant was conserved between humans and mice (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by conservation analysis using BLAST.

claim: The rates of morphological normality of sperm decreased to zero in 7 of 19 patients harbouring CYLC1 variant.
source: The rates of morphological normality of sperm decreased to zero in 7 of 19 patients harbouring CYLC1 variant, and the remaining affected individuals had a morphological normality rate of less than 4% (Barratt et al., 2017; Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by semen analysis data from patients.

claim: The remaining 12 affected individuals harbouring CYLC1 variant had a morphological normality rate of less than 4%.
source: The rates of morphological normality of sperm decreased to zero in 7 of 19 patients harbouring CYLC1 variant, and the remaining affected individuals had a morphological normality rate of less than 4% (Barratt et al., 2017; Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by semen analysis data from patients.

claim: Sperm from men harbouring CYLC1 variant displayed deformed acrosomes as revealed by Papanicolaou staining.
source: In the healthy control, the acrosome covered more than one-third of the anterior sperm head; in contrast, sperm from men harbouring CYLC1 variant displayed deformed acrosomes (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Papanicolaou staining and microscopy analysis.

claim: The PT-PAR distribution of cylicin-1 was disrupted and the acrosomes were deformed in sperm from patients harbouring CYLC1 variant.
source: Costaining of PNA-FITC and cylicin-1 indicated that the PT-PAR distribution of cylicin-1 was disrupted and the acrosomes were deformed in sperm from patients harbouring CYLC1 variant (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence costaining data.

claim: TEM analysis revealed that acrosomes were detached in sperm from patients harbouring CYLC1 variant.
source: TEM analysis clearly revealed that acrosomes were detached in sperm from patients harbouring CYLC1 variant (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM imaging of patient sperm samples.

claim: Cylc1-mutant mice carrying a single amino acid change equivalent to the variant in human CYLC1 were generated using CRISPR/Cas9 technology.
source: We next generated Cylc1-mutant mice that carried a single amino acid change equivalent to the variant in human CYLC1 using CRISPR/Cas9 technology (Figure 6A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the mouse generation strategy and sequencing confirmation.

claim: Cylc1-mutant mice were male subfertile.
source: Cylc1-mutant mice grew normally but were male subfertile.
evidence: The claim is supported by fertility testing data.

claim: Of the 42 female mice mated with WT males, 35 were pregnant and gave rise to 281 offspring.
source: Of the 42 female mice mated with WT males, 35 were pregnant and gave rise to 281 offspring.
evidence: The claim is supported by fertility testing data.

claim: Of the 28 female mice mated with Cylc1-mutant males, only 11 were pregnant, giving rise to 49 offspring.
source: In contrast, of the 28 female mice mated with Cylc1-mutant males, only 11 were pregnant, giving rise to 49 offspring (Figure 6C, D).
evidence: The claim is supported by fertility testing data.

claim: Cylc1-mutant mice and WT mice showed similar testis sizes and weights.
source: Cylc1-mutant mice and WT mice showed similar testis sizes and weights (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological measurements.

claim: Spermatogenesis and sperm production were generally normal in Cylc1-mutant mice as indicated by H&E staining.
source: Spermatogenesis and sperm production were generally normal, as indicated by hematoxylin–eosin staining of the testis and cauda epididymis from Cylc1-mutant mice and WT mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological analysis.

claim: The sperm count and total motility of Cylc1-mutant mice were similar to those indexes in WT mice.
source: Further examination showed that the sperm count and total motility of Cylc1-mutant mice were similar to those indexes in WT mice (Figure 6E, F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative sperm analysis.

claim: Cylc1-mutant mice produced sperm with abnormal head morphologies, exhibiting varying degrees of 'fan-shaped' heads.
source: Similar to Cylc1-KO mice, Cylc1-mutant mice produced sperm with abnormal head morphologies, exhibiting varying degrees of 'fan-shaped' heads (Figure 6G).
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological analysis of sperm.

claim: Spermatids from Cylc1-mutant mice exhibited varying degrees of acrosome detachment.
source: Compared with the closely attached acrosomes in WT mice, spermatids from Cylc1-mutant mice exhibited varying degrees of acrosome detachment (Figure 6H).
evidence: The claim is supported by PNA-FITC staining and microscopy analysis.

claim: Spermatids of Cylc1-mutant mice showed uneven, thin, or ectopic F-actin distribution.
source: The F-actin bundles of spermatid heads in WT mice possessed typical fibrous textures, whereas spermatids of Cylc1-mutant mice showed uneven, thin, or ectopic F-actin distribution (Figure 6H).
evidence: The claim is supported by F-actin staining and microscopy analysis.

claim: TEM analysis of elongating spermatids within the testis revealed an enlarged space area between the IAM and the NE in Cylc1-mutant mice.
source: TEM analysis of elongating spermatids within the testis revealed an enlarged space area between the IAM and the NE in Cylc1-mutant mice (Figure 6I).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM imaging of testis tissues.

claim: The CYLC1 variant did not obviously affect the protein expression of cylicin-1 and its interactors.
source: Although this variant did not obviously affect the protein expression of cylicin-1 and its interactors, the endogenous interaction between cylicin-1 and ACTL7A was attenuated in testis lysates of Cylc1-mutant mice (Figure 6J).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot analysis.

claim: The endogenous interaction between cylicin-1 and ACTL7A was attenuated in testis lysates of Cylc1-mutant mice.
source: Although this variant did not obviously affect the protein expression of cylicin-1 and its interactors, the endogenous interaction between cylicin-1 and ACTL7A was attenuated in testis lysates of Cylc1-mutant mice (Figure 6J).
evidence: The claim is supported by endogenous co-IP experiments.

claim: The protein–protein interaction of cylicin-1 and IAM protein SPACA1 in testis lysates was weakened in Cylc1-mutant mice.
source: The protein‒protein interaction of cylicin-1 and IAM protein SPACA1 in testis lysates was also weakened in Cylc1-mutant mice (Figure 6K).
evidence: The claim is supported by endogenous co-IP experiments.

claim: Mutation of cylicin-1 affected the endogenous interaction between ACTL7A and SPACA1.
source: Moreover, mutation of cylicin-1 affected the endogenous interaction between ACTL7A and SPACA1 (Figure 6L).
evidence: The claim is supported by endogenous co-IP experiments.

claim: Two-cell embryos and blastocysts could be obtained upon ICSI using sperm from Cylc1-KO male mice with a similar efficiency to that from WT male mice.
source: We further conducted intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) experiments and found that two-cell embryos and blastocysts could be obtained upon ICSI using sperm from Cylc1-KO male mice with a similar efficiency to that from WT male mice (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by ICSI experimental data.

claim: ICSI but not IVF could serve as a promising treatment for patients carrying CYLC1 variants.
source: Consistent with the observations in mice, ART for patients carrying CYLC1 variant indicated that ICSI but not IVF could serve as a promising treatment (Table 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by clinical ART outcome data.

claim: For patients AAW228, AAG547, AAX199, BBB654, BBB841, AAT812, 3307, and 3256, IVF treatments all failed, whereas ICSI treatment generated good-quality embryos.
source: For patients AAW228, AAG547, AAX199, BBB654, BBB841, AAT812, 3307, and 3256, IVF treatments all failed, whereas ICSI treatment (with or without assisted oocyte activation AOA) generated good-quality embryos.
evidence: The claim is supported by clinical ART outcome data.

claim: Live birth and pregnancy was obtained from individuals AAW228, AAG547, AAT812, 3307, and 3256 after ICSI treatment.
source: Live birth and pregnancy was finally obtained from individuals AAW228, AAG547, AAT812, 3307, and 3256.
evidence: The claim is supported by clinical ART outcome data.

claim: Live birth was acquired for individuals AAX765, BBA344, BBA396, 3086, 3165, 3190, 3203, and 3010 after ICSI and embryo transplantation.
source: Finally, live birth was acquired for individuals AAX765, BBA344, BBA396, 3086, 3165, 3190, 3203, and 3010 after embryo transplantation.
evidence: The claim is supported by clinical ART outcome data.

claim: The perinuclear theca (PT) is a dense cytoplasmic web encapsulating the sperm nucleus.
source: The perinuclear theca (PT) is a dense cytoplasmic web encapsulating the sperm nucleus.
evidence: The claim is a definitional statement about PT structure.

claim: The PT is a detergent- and high salt-resistant structure.
source: In mammalian sperm, the cytoskeletal element encapsulating the nuclei is a detergent- and high salt-resistant structure called the perinuclear theca (PT) (Oko and Sutovsky, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Apically, the PT resides between the inner acrosomal membrane (IAM) and the nuclear envelope (NE) making up the subacrosomal layer (PT-SAL).
source: Apically, the PT resides between the inner acrosomal membrane (IAM) and the nuclear envelope (NE) making up the subacrosomal layer (PT-SAL, also known as the acroplaxome), while caudally, it resides between the cell membrane and the NE making up the postacrosomal part (PT-PAR, also known as the calyx).
evidence: The claim describes the anatomical location of PT-SAL.

claim: Caudally, the PT resides between the cell membrane and the NE making up the postacrosomal part (PT-PAR).
source: Apically, the PT resides between the inner acrosomal membrane (IAM) and the nuclear envelope (NE) making up the subacrosomal layer (PT-SAL, also known as the acroplaxome), while caudally, it resides between the cell membrane and the NE making up the postacrosomal part (PT-PAR, also known as the calyx).
evidence: The claim describes the anatomical location of PT-PAR.

claim: Two kinds of basic proteins, calicin and cylicins, are the major constituents of PT as determined by Longo et al.
source: Longo et al. determined that two kinds of basic proteins are the major constituents of PT: calicin and cylicins (Longo et al., 1987).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: More than 20 PT-enriched proteins have been identified from mammalian sperm.
source: After that, more than 20 PT-enriched proteins, such as fatty acid-binding protein (FABP)9 (Oko and Morales, 1994), actin-capping protein (CP) α3/β3 (von Bülow et al., 1997), transcription factor STAT4 (Herrada and Wolgemuth, 1997), actin-related proteins ACTRT1/2 (Heid et al., 2002), histone H2B variant H2BL1 (Aul and Oko, 2002), sperm-borne oocyte activating factors (PLCζ and PAWP) (Aarabi et al., 2014; Hachem et al., 2017), and the glutathione S-transferase GSTO2 (Hamilton et al., 2017), have been identified from mammalian sperm.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The PT is speculated to function as an architectural element involved in the shape changes of the nucleus during spermiogenesis.
source: The PT is speculated to function as (1) an architectural element involved in the shape changes of the nucleus during spermiogenesis, (2) a cement linking the acrosome with the nucleus, and (3) a candidate for sperm-borne oocyte activation.
evidence: The claim is a speculative statement about PT function.

claim: The PT is speculated to function as a cement linking the acrosome with the nucleus.
source: The PT is speculated to function as (1) an architectural element involved in the shape changes of the nucleus during spermiogenesis, (2) a cement linking the acrosome with the nucleus, and (3) a candidate for sperm-borne oocyte activation.
evidence: The claim is a speculative statement about PT function.

claim: The PT is speculated to be a candidate for sperm-borne oocyte activation.
source: The PT is speculated to function as (1) an architectural element involved in the shape changes of the nucleus during spermiogenesis, (2) a cement linking the acrosome with the nucleus, and (3) a candidate for sperm-borne oocyte activation.
evidence: The claim is a speculative statement about PT function.

claim: Loss of calicin specifically leads to the surface subsidence of sperm heads in the nuclear condensation stage.
source: Loss of calicin specifically leads to the surface subsidence of sperm heads in the nuclear condensation stage (Zhang et al., 2022a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Three infertile men with sperm head deformities carry homozygous pathogenic mutations in CCIN.
source: Importantly, we further report that three infertile men with sperm head deformities carry homozygous pathogenic mutations in CCIN, and the corresponding Ccin-mutant mice mimic the phenotype in patients (Fan et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Actrt1-KO male mice are severely subfertile as a result of detached acrosomes and fertilization deficiency.
source: Actrt1-KO male mice are severely subfertile as a result of detached acrosomes and fertilization deficiency (Zhang et al., 2022b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: ACTRT1 anchors acrosomes to the nucleus by interacting with some IAM proteins and NE proteins.
source: ACTRT1 anchors acrosomes to the nucleus by interacting with some IAM proteins and NE proteins (Zhang et al., 2022b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Cylicin-1 is a 74 kDa protein that contains numerous lysine dipeptides followed by a third variable amino acid (KKX).
source: 74 kDa cylicin-1 contains numerous lysine dipeptides followed by a third variable amino acid (KKX).
evidence: The claim describes the structural features of cylicin-1.

claim: The C-terminal tail of cylicin-1 contains proline-rich segments.
source: The C-terminal tail contains proline-rich segments and the central portion of the protein is arranged as a series of repeating units that are predicted to form short alpha helices.
evidence: The claim describes the structural features of cylicin-1.

claim: The central portion of cylicin-1 is arranged as a series of repeating units that are predicted to form short alpha helices.
source: The C-terminal tail contains proline-rich segments and the central portion of the protein is arranged as a series of repeating units that are predicted to form short alpha helices.
evidence: The claim describes the structural features of cylicin-1 based on sequence analysis.

claim: Northern blotting detects the cylicin-1 transcript only in the testis.
source: Northern blotting detects the cylicin-1 transcript only in the testis, and an antibody against cylicin-1 specifically stains the PT-PAR of human and bovine sperm (Hess et al., 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: An antibody against cylicin-1 specifically stains the PT-PAR of human and bovine sperm.
source: Northern blotting detects the cylicin-1 transcript only in the testis, and an antibody against cylicin-1 specifically stains the PT-PAR of human and bovine sperm (Hess et al., 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Cylicin-1 mediates the acrosome–nucleus connection across species.
source: Our experimental observations indicate that cylicin-1 mediates the acrosome–nucleus connection across species, and importantly, CYLC1 variants are linked to male in/subfertility (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from both mouse models and human patients.

claim: CYLC1 variants are linked to male in/subfertility.
